topics.topic: Monotonic instant representation and microsecond precision
questions: In what representation are monotonic instants stored and compared, including the precision required by the microsecond boundary test?
What exact representation and precision must hold monotonic instants and support duration arithmetic, especially the one-microsecond boundary required by test 8?
In what representation and precision are monotonic instants stored and compared so that the microsecond boundary in Required test 8 has a defined result?

quotes:
One reading in nanoseconds, comparable only with other readings of the same
process.

Every limit of A13 — 8 hours, 30, 15 and 10 minutes, 60 seconds — is
measured between two of these readings and never by the wall clock.
judgement.why: The later clock operation fixes monotonic readings as nanoseconds, which preserves the required microsecond distinction.

topics.topic: Per-operation monotonic and wall-clock sampling and sharing
questions: How many monotonic and UTC wall-clock readings does each operation take, and which effects of one operation must share the same reading?
How many monotonic and wall-clock readings does each operation take, and which single reading, if any, governs all checks and timestamps in that operation or cleanup pass?
How many monotonic and UTC wall-clock readings does each operation take, and which checks and written instants within that operation must share one reading?

judgement.why: P2 asks the same question about per-operation clock sampling and sharing, and the relevant passages have not changed since that judgement.

precedent.topic: Per-operation clock sampling policy and which checks or timestamps share a captured reading
quotes:
- **Time.** An action has one instant: `operations` reads it from
  `clock.recorded_now` once, when the action's transaction begins, with
  today's date (`clock.today_in_utc`), and hands both to every module the
  action records a new instant or compares a date in. The import's records
  keep the instants their source holds ("Revisions and times"); the Customers
  it makes, its closure and its entry carry the action's one instant. The
  limits of A13 are read by `owner_sessions` from `clock.monotonic_reading`;
  the minute look of A18 rule 1 by `backups` from `clock.recorded_now`; a
  backup's instant is the one `store` reads at the read that fixes the
  copy's snapshot (A18 rule 1), which `backups` records and never reads
  itself; `instance_lifecycle` times its two passes by
  `clock.monotonic_reading`. No other module reads a clock.

A new owner session (M11) with its sign-in reading of
`clock.monotonic_reading`, no pending confirmation and no uploaded file; the
refusal count cleared. A refused sign-in outside a lockout counts at its
reading; the fifth less than 15 minutes old starts a 15-minute lockout.

At its arrival a request carrying a valid session restarts the session's
30 minutes, whatever its answer — a CSRF refusal included; of concurrent
arrivals the latest counts (A13 rule 2). A sign-out's admission marks the
session signed out at once.

The session's pending confirmation is replaced: a new value from
`random_values.make_secret_value`, bound to the action, its target, what the
step showed and the digest of its inputs in a fixed order, and the reading
of `clock.monotonic_reading` it was shown at.

The pass alone
ends sessions by their limits: it takes the import lock, reads
`clock.monotonic_reading` once, and decides every session by that one
reading, in the order of their sign-in, each under its own lock, so the
order decides nothing.
precedent.why: The later module and public-operation texts assign one recorded action instant to every persisted fact and date comparison and separately fix the readings used by sign-in, request arrival, confirmation display and the expiry pass.

Every publish and every withdrawal on one project's pointers is
   serialised with the others: each runs on the result of the one before, in
   the order their transactions take the store's one write lock, which is
   also the order they commit in; that order is the first and the second.

   accepted with consecutive

   refused as withdrawing a superseded pointer; a publish that runs after a
   withdrawal makes the next version `published`; a second withdrawal of one

changes to A01, A04 and A07 name constants and an exception of the
mapping's stage (4), and A07's concurrent publishes are those of different

topics.topic: Sign-in critical-section boundaries for credential checks and clock reads
questions: Does a sign-in take the sign-in lock before checking the credential and reading the monotonic clock, or are those performed before the lock and only the count, decision and update protected?

quotes:
Registry counts the sign-ins refused for a wrong or missing credential
   whose instant is less than 15 minutes before now, for the whole instance:
   Registry tells no callers apart by address (R0-27). The fifth such refusal
   starts a lockout that lasts while now is less than 15 minutes after that
   refusal. During the lockout every sign-in is refused — the right credential
   included — and is not counted; the lockout is not extended. A successful
   sign-in clears the count. Count and lockout are runtime state, like the
   owner session, and a restart clears them. Concurrent sign-ins are counted
   one at a time, in the order they take the instance's one sign-in lock,
   under which each reads the count, decides and updates it.

A refused sign-in answers the same whatever was wrong, and never echoes
   the credential. Sign-in is the one owner request made without a session:
   it is checked for the credential and the lockout only, carries no CSRF
   value, and the session cookie it sets is sent only to Registry's origin
   (rule 1).
judgement.divergence: One implementation acquires the sign-in lock before credential comparison and makes the earlier wrong attempt the fifth refusal, while another compares credentials before lock acquisition and lets the later correct attempt acquire the lock first and clear the count; the owner attempting the correct sign-in sees refusal versus a new session.
judgement.why: The text serializes reading the count, deciding and updating it but does not place credential comparison or the attempt's monotonic reading relative to acquisition of the sign-in lock.

witness.initial: The instance has four wrong-credential refusals less than fifteen minutes old and no lockout.
events: A caller starts a fifth sign-in with a wrong credential and its credential comparison has not completed.
The owner starts a concurrent sign-in with the right credential.
Registry orders the attempts according to the implementation's placement of credential comparison relative to the sign-in lock.
outcomes: If the wrong attempt holds the lock while its credential is checked, it records the fifth refusal and starts the lockout; the owner's right credential is refused.

If credential comparison occurs before lock acquisition, the owner's verified attempt can take the lock first, succeed and clear the four refusals; the wrong attempt later becomes the first new refusal.
witness.observer: The owner using the right credential
basis:
The owner signs in with the owner credential (R0-30) and receives an owner
   session (M11), carried by a cookie that scripts cannot read, sent only over
   HTTPS when the interface is reached from another machine (R0-29), and only
   to Registry's own origin.

Registry counts the sign-ins refused for a wrong or missing credential
   whose instant is less than 15 minutes before now, for the whole instance:
   Registry tells no callers apart by address (R0-27). The fifth such refusal
   starts a lockout that lasts while now is less than 15 minutes after that
   refusal. During the lockout every sign-in is refused — the right credential
   included — and is not counted; the lockout is not extended. A successful
   sign-in clears the count. Count and lockout are runtime state, like the
   owner session, and a restart clears them. Concurrent sign-ins are counted
   one at a time, in the order they take the instance's one sign-in lock,
   under which each reads the count, decides and updates it.

topics.topic: Whether a request after expiry triggers session cleanup or only refusal
questions: After a limit has been reached but before the cleanup pass, does the next request merely get refused, or does that request itself end the session and drop its pending confirmation and upload?

quotes:
A session that has reached a
   limit serves no request from that
   moment: a request carrying it is refused at the session check. Registry
   ends it — and drops its pending confirmation and its uploaded file with it
   (M11) — at a pass over the sessions it makes every 60 seconds from the
   start; the pass alone ends sessions by their limits, taking the import
   lock and then each session's lock (A16 rule 2) and deciding under them.

With the clocks replaced in the test: moving the wall clock back or
   forward by hours changes no session's validity; a suspension of 31
   minutes, counted by the monotonic reading, ends the session at its next
   request.
judgement.why: The wording suggests different cleanup times, but the texts provide no operation or caller-visible observation of an invalid session's pending confirmation or uploaded file between the refused request and the next cleanup pass, so no admissible observable witness can be built.

questions: Are successful or refused agent-authority reads audited, or are all of them covered by the rule that ordinary reads are not recorded?

topics.topic: Whether the sign-in refusal limit is an imported constant or literal rule
questions: Is `SIGN_IN_REFUSAL_LIMIT` also the data provider's imported constant, or is five a literal rule that implementations may encode directly?
